paragraphs: When Fu Rong arrived outside the garrison town at Anding and found its gates shut, his first order was to raise his banner high.

The black Qin flag snapped in the spring wind. There was a Qin flag on the battlements too, its corner stitched with the new unit number assigned by the central army command. Between the two banners lay a ditch and a drawbridge. Crossbowmen held bolts against their strings. Neither side was willing to be the first to call the other comrades.

There was still no good news from the sickbed in Luoyang. Fu Rong had traveled west from the palace for seven days, hearing seven different accounts of his imperial brother’s death along the way. He had handed each rumor-monger to the local magistrate to trace the source. Only at Anding had he heard the indisputable news that two women had died inside a Qin garrison.
“Is Du Yan on the wall?”
A gaunt face appeared behind the parapet. Du Yan was about fifty, deep-eyed and still wearing a uniform he had not changed in days. He saluted Fu Rong but gave no order to lower the bridge.

Fu Rong ordered a military clerk to read aloud the document bearing the three seals. Du Yan was suspended pending inquiry; the imprisoned families of soldiers were to be released at once; the garrison’s defenses were provisionally placed under the deputy commandant. As the last clause was read, several men on the wall stole glances at Du Yan’s face.

“Duke of Yangping,” Du Yan called, “White Grass Valley is less than a hundred li away, and Yao Chang’s vanguard has crossed the valley mouth. Open the gates now and the Qiang inside will set fires and welcome the rebels.”
“Whom have you seen preparing a fire?”
“We have reports.”
“From whom?”
Du Yan hesitated. “Men who escaped back here.”

Fu Rong asked how many days the grain and fodder within the walls would last. Du Yan said at least fifteen. Fu Rong did not argue more loudly. He had the rear column unload its supplies and camp beneath the wall, and sent military physicians and water carts to the gate first.
“There are more than a thousand women and children confined inside,” he called up. “Some must be ill. You need not let me enter. Let the physicians in first.”

Silence followed on the wall. Several guards muttered among themselves. At last a bamboo basket came down and took the medicine bundles up, but no man was admitted. Fu Rong did not order the siege ladders forward. He feared that once blades were drawn, this town, whose men still called themselves Qin soldiers, would never again find anyone willing to sheathe his weapon first.

Smoke rose inside the walls that afternoon. In the sheds of the horse yard where the families were held, several children had lit dry grass in the hope of drawing attention from outside. The fire was small, but smoke spread from the enclosure across half a street. Du Yan ordered it extinguished. The men guarding the yard rushed first to protect their own weapons, leaving women to drag water buckets back and forth. Some ran to the shed gate demanding it be unlocked; the sentries, acting under orders, barred them. The quarrel grew fiercer.
A Qiang soldier on the battlements threw his bow at his feet and shouted to the men below, “Duke of Yangping! My mother is in that horse yard too!”

Du Yan ordered his personal guards to seize him. Other Qiang soldiers stepped in their way. A helmet fell on the bricks and rolled to the feet of a Di soldier. He stooped to pick it up, intending to hand it back, but with swords gripped on both sides he could only stand there helplessly.
Fu Rong heard the cries from within and raised his arm to stop his own army from drawing its bows.
“Du Yan. Release them first. If you fear an uprising tonight, keep troops on the parade ground. I will answer for you.”
“Can the duke answer for what lies in their hearts?”
“No. I can answer for the written order to open the gates.”

In the end it was the deputy commandant who opened them. Hearing the drawbridge winch turn, Du Yan wheeled around to stop him, but several veterans who had stood guard beside him seized and held him. One old soldier wept. “General, the town is nearly burning. For pity’s sake, let the children out first.”

When the bridge came down, Fu Rong did not rush his army in. He entered with only five hundred men. He sent the physicians straight to the horse yard, handed Du Yan to the military judicial officers, and ordered the existing company officers to remain in place until their units could be checked. The opening of the gate brought no immediate cheering. Women emerged from the enclosure carrying children, keeping away from armed men. Only at the street corner did one suddenly fall to her knees and begin to sob.

Two bodies wrapped in white cloth lay beside the courtyard wall. Liang Agui hurried from the left camp and recognized his wife’s old boots at a glance. He had sewn the patch at one ankle the winter before, in clumsy, ugly stitches. She had laughed at his poor hands all that day. Now he reached out and touched the seam without crying or speaking.
“Who fired the arrow?”
A nearby soldier pointed to a sentry standing with his head lowered. The man had been bound and kept repeating that his orders were simply to prevent anyone leaving the yard.

Liang Agui took two steps toward him before a military judge stopped him. Fu Rong stood nearby and offered no words of comfort. He asked Liang to distinguish what he had seen with his own eyes from what neighbors had told him, while a clerk took down his words.
“She went out to ask for water,” Liang Agui said. “She was carrying our child. The boy lived.”
Only after he said it did he ask suddenly, “Where is the child?”

Beyond the courtyard gate a little boy pressed himself against his aunt, a military robe much too large for him draped over his shoulders. Liang Agui went to him and crouched halfway to lift him, but the boy recoiled as though he did not know his father. Only days earlier Liang had commanded a unit and could distinguish friend from enemy amid the beating of drums. Now he had forgotten even how to pick up his own son.

Fu Rong granted him half a day for the funeral rites. In front of Liang and the military judge, he wrote down a deadline for reexamining the deaths and holding an open hearing. Liang asked, “When the fighting begins, will Your Grace still remember that deadline?”
Fu Rong offered him the brush. “Write it on the back yourself. If the case has not been heard by then, bring this to the military office and find me.”
Liang Agui could not write a graceful hand. He managed one crooked stroke of his surname. That made the military order heavier than many imperial edicts.

The next day Murong Chui came to Anding with three hundred horsemen. The crown prince had authorized him to assist in reorganizing the mixed army for the western campaign; Fu Rong remained commander, and any movement of more than five thousand men required fresh verification of the order. Fu Rong read the edict and asked why Murong Chui had not stayed in Hebei.

“The floodwaters have gone down there. The fields remain, and so do the people quarreling over them,” Murong Chui replied. “There are officials to deal with those matters now. Here, at least, I know which army is waiting for the other.”

They spread a map of White Grass Valley across the command table. Yao Chang’s men had taken several valley mouths. Tribal banners gathered in clusters, but no great force had yet assaulted the town. Murong Chui pointed out that what Yao most wanted was not to storm Anding but to see another body of Qiang soldiers desert. If Qin’s ranks broke from within, he could spare himself a hard battle.

Fu Rong ordered the company officers to muster every unit without regrouping men by clan or people. Several Di commanders were uneasy and suggested holding the Qiang soldiers in the rear for now. Murong Chui did not deliver a speech about loyalty. He simply asked, “If you move them away, who will take their place holding the half of the shield wall they know?”

One company commander pointed at the deployment map but could not answer. Men had been transferred between companies for years. The soldier who knew his neighbor’s drum calls might not share his birthplace. Murong Chui replaced the unit flags in their original positions and ordered the clerks to check their old rolls again: who could use a bow, who knew the waterways, who could mend horse tack. They would fill genuine gaps, not remove a man because his name sounded like someone else’s.

That night scouts captured three spies carrying letters. The handwriting suggested a government scribe. Each note named the whereabouts of some officer’s wife and children, or which camp held his brothers. The letter to Liang Agui had been written by his younger brother, Liang Abao. Its last line used the familiar dialect of their childhood: “Brother, Sister-in-law died by Qin hands. Come back.”
Fu Rong returned the letter to Liang Agui and asked whether he wanted to go.
Liang studied it a long time. “I do.”
A Di general at once gripped his sword. Fu Rong merely asked, “What would you go to do?”
“I’d like to shake some sense into my brother. And ask Yao Chang who told him to set up a mourning shrine for my wife. She never knew Yao Chang while she lived.”
“Then you won’t lead a unit tonight,” Fu Rong said. “The funeral is not yet over. Sleep behind the tents tonight. If you still want to lead your bowmen in the morning, we’ll talk then.”

Liang Agui’s face darkened; he thought his command was being taken from him. Fu Rong laid Liang’s bow on the table. “I’m not confiscating it. I’m asking you not to loose an arrow tonight that you will regret for the rest of your life.”

Nevertheless, forty-seven men deserted the Qin army that night. Some climbed the palisade; several horsemen killed a groom to steal mounts. The clerk who reported the count trembled as he suggested bringing the families of Qiang troops into the garrison, both to prevent contact with the enemy and to make fugitives easier to trace. Fu Rong had already begun writing the order. He reached the words “families to remain temporarily” just as Murong Chui entered from outside the tent.
“Isn’t that what Du Yan just did?”
Fu Rong looked up, his gaze turning cold. “Have you come to teach me how to command troops?”
“I’ve come to ask you to set down your brush a moment.”
“Men deserted tonight.”
“Men deserted. Not their wives and children.”

They argued bitterly. Fu Rong thought of the enemy banners outside and the dead still unburied within the walls. Murong Chui’s mild words almost made him laugh with anger. But Murong Chui knew that if families were seized, every Qiang soldier still at his post would see the lesson: one man deserts and those left behind are punished first. They had watched the very same thing at the town gate the night before.

At last Fu Rong tore the document apart. The new order provided only for pursuing the deserters themselves and trying those against whom there was proof under military law. Their families could go to market as usual; any household found concealing weapons or passing messages would be investigated separately. Murong Chui gathered up the torn paper and gave it to a clerk to burn, lest half a sheet escape and be treated as a genuine order.

As the army marched west, the Anding garrison kept its market open each day. Vanguard, center, and rearguard stretched in a long column beyond the walls. Beneath the banners marched Di shield-bearers, Xianbei horsemen, Han crossbowmen, and Qiang archers. Liang Agui did not immediately rejoin his company but traveled with the center. The earth on his wife’s new grave was still wet. He knew his brother stood across the lines. He knew too that his son was waiting for him in Anding.

Below White Horse Slope, Yao’s cavalry rode back and forth over the grass, calling names across the hills. Some shouted the childhood nicknames of Qin soldiers; others displayed letters from their relatives. One rider even lifted a woman’s bloodstained clothes. Wherever a shout landed, soldiers' eyes followed. A young Qiang archer protested anxiously that he knew no one on the western side. His company commander simply ordered him back into line. Beside him a Di soldier muttered that the more he protested, the more suspicious he sounded. The two nearly drew blades on each other.

Fu Rong passed by and punished both men under military law, as well as their commander for failing to keep order. He did not ask which people either belonged to. Yet when the young Qiang was struck with the rod, he still glared bitterly at the Di man beside him; the fairness of the punishment could not instantly erase his grievance.

Watching from west of the river, Yao Chang was pleased. He ordered deserters who knew Qin camp signals to prepare false banners, while the tribes guarded the pasture and water assigned to them. Yao Shuode asked whether three thousand Qiang soldiers in the Qin ranks truly meant to defect. Yao studied the list. “All forty-seven guides who came over say thousands more want to run. A man who has just left always wants to believe he wasn’t the only one.”
“Then how many are there really?”
“We’ll find out when we fight.”
“Will my lord stake the vanguard on it?”
“I’ll stake it on their doubts.” Yao pointed toward the Qin Qiang archers. “Once the banners are confused, they’ll drive one another out for us.”

The next morning mist still hung over the shallow river as the armies formed on opposite banks. The western banners were a jumble of tribal red, yellow, blue, and white, crossing in the wind. Those on the eastern bank were plain by comparison, marked mostly with company and battalion numbers. Yao Chang rode to the water’s edge and called across to Fu Rong: “Your elder brother is too ill to speak. Whom does Qin obey now?”
“The Secretariat governs, the central army command issues orders, and the crown prince acts as regent,” Fu Rong answered from the far bank.
“I asked who’s sitting on the dragon throne.”
“When he wakes, he’ll know what we have defended.”

Yao Chang did not prolong the exchange. He ordered Liang Abao forward to call to his elder brother. Abao raised his sister-in-law’s bloodstained garment. Wind lifted the edge of its sleeve, showing a patch of stitching exactly as Liang Agui remembered it.
When Liang Agui came forward, he wore neither armor nor bow. Fu Rong rode alongside but did not ask whether he had changed his mind.
“Abao,” Liang Agui shouted across the river, “have you been home?”
“I can’t go back! They’ll kill me!”
“Were you there when we buried your sister-in-law?”
Abao’s eyes flickered. He said nothing.
“When they shut her in the horse yard, the family still owed five dou of millet. Is the grain you’ve taken enough even to feed yourself?”
His younger brother grew agitated. “General Yao says we’ll get land after victory. Everything will be provided!”
“Whose land? Who’s farming it now?”
Liang Abao looked toward Yao Chang. Yao gave no answer. He could hardly settle the question of land redistribution in a shouted conversation across a river.

Then Liang Agui stopped shouting at his brother. He turned and pointed to the Qin ranks behind him. “The day we buried her, Di soldiers carried her coffin for me. A Xianbei physician examined her body, and a Han army clerk surnamed Zhao helped settle my child. I used to curse those men myself. Now that your sister-in-law is dead, which one do you want me to kill as an enemy?”

Behind the shields on the eastern bank came several dull knocks. A few men were gently striking the earth with the butts of their spears. Others joined in, without rhythm or order. Liang looked back and saw his old company still behind its flag. Some men there had never known his wife; others had shared the same bowl of bitter medicine with him.
Yao Chang could wait no longer without losing his chance. He struck the war drum with sudden force.

The first arrows fell into the water. Cavalry at the front charged down the riverbank, their horses sinking into the mud while the ranks behind kept pressing forward. Qin crossbows gave a brief hum from between the shields. Murong Chui led his cavalry upstream around the left flank; Yao’s concealed mounted archers came to meet him, and the two forces tangled among the stubble of old reeds.

Yao’s true target was several units in the Qin front line with large numbers of Qiang troops. Deserters in old Qin armor rode down the side slope beneath matching unit banners, shouting, “The left camp has surrendered!” An arrow struck a standard-bearer, and his flag tumbled with the horse into a shallow ditch. Several companies saw only the fallen flag and rising dust and believed the neighboring units had actually run over to Yao. The line split down the middle.

Some Qiang archers threw down their bows and ran backward; Han soldiers retreated with them. Di cavalry saw the vanguard give way and, without asking why, spurred forward to block their retreat. Liang Agui seized a riderless horse and planted himself in their path, shouting for them to stop. The cavalry commander cursed him: the runners were traitors, and unless they were cut down the whole army would dissolve.
“They’ve lost order. They haven’t all rebelled!” Liang Agui loosed an arrow into the wet ground before the cavalry. “If you charge among them, our own men will kill our own men!”

The cavalry commander already had his sword raised, but several riders recognized Liang Agui. A Qiang man whose wife had just been buried could have slipped away during the night if he had wanted to leave; instead he was blocking their path. For a moment no one dared charge first. At last the central banner emerged through the dust. Fu Rong rode up in person and ordered the crossbowmen to withdraw half an arrow’s range, every unit to re-form beneath its original standard, and no man to pursue or kill soldiers who had lost formation.

Some heard the calls and returned; others kept running. Barely more than two hundred crossed the river to join Yao. Stragglers gradually regained their places, the break in the line closing inch by inch like a rent sewn shut. When the second wave of Yao’s horsemen arrived, they met a shield wall raised once more.

West of the river, Yao Chang saw the trouble. The tribal chiefs had agreed to enter the water by turns. After the first two contingents suffered heavy losses, those behind hesitated. Some complained of insufficient fodder; others claimed their turn had not yet come. The gaps between banners grew ever wider. While Yao pressed them to attack, a messenger knelt with a report: the Liang contingent on the right insisted that the Yao household troops must cross first.
“What did they promise when they swore the alliance?” Yao Shuode demanded angrily.

The messenger did not dare answer. Yao Chang saw a yellow banner on the heights edging quietly backward and knew that more urging would do no good. He raised his head to listen to the wind. Mixed with the battle drums were different retreat calls sounding from his own camps. When the army first gathered, he had thought a multitude of banners meant strength. Now he saw that every banner gave someone a reason not to advance.

Murong Chui had broken the upstream ambush and was coming against their rear flank. Some former Yan soldiers recognized him and cried “Prince of Wu!” across their horses. He did not even turn his head, ordering his riders to cut off the grain carts first and forbidding pursuit without orders. Yao’s flank dissolved faster. Two tribes guarding the ford crowded onto the same stony bank; banners fell, and fugitives crossed over the bodies floating in the water.

Yao Chang cut down a unit leader who withdrew first, but could not stop the men behind from finding other routes. Yao Shuode urged him to enter the northern valley and save the household cavalry. Yao wiped the blood from his blade on his horse’s mane and finally turned away.

Mounted reinforcements had been meant to guard the escape route. At the valley entrance only embers remained. The tribal chief responsible had taken his men and left, abandoning a line scrawled in charcoal beside the fire: “The Yao family’s war is not our people’s war.” Yao Shuode angrily wanted to pursue them. Yao Chang rode over the words without another curse.

The mountain rain came suddenly. Fugitives abandoned grain wagons; rain-soaked leather grew heavy, horses slipped off the stone ledges, and most of the remaining household troops scattered. A guide led them west, but when Yao Chang asked twice how far it was, the man gave vague answers. At last he confessed that Qin troops already held the western exit and his tribal chief had ordered him to mislead the Yao party. He had barely prostrated himself before Yao Shuode stabbed him to death. Yao Chang did not intervene. He took the reins and headed north. Ten li farther on a landslide had sealed the road with mud and stone.

At daybreak Qin voices calling for surrender echoed from outside the valley. Yao Chang tried to take the hundred or so guards who could still walk and climb the slope, but the wounded clutched at his horse’s legs, weeping and asking whether their lord meant to abandon them.
“They say Qin soldiers will kill every Qiang!” a wounded man shouted. “It’s written in the proclamation!”
Yao Chang opened his mouth to say the Qin army might spare men who surrendered. Then he found his own lie standing in his path: no one would believe him if he tried to change the story now.

Murong Chui’s troops appeared on the slope. Several Xianbei riders had dismounted to form a shield line, Han soldiers stood beside them with crossbows, and a Qiang military physician was calling for the wounded not to move. Yao Shuode led two charges and lost dozens of men. When he drew his sword for a third, Yao Chang seized his wrist. “Enough.”
“My lord, capture means death.”
“If you think death is certain, then watch me die first.”

Yao Chang released his sword hilt. The short blade that had followed him out of Chang’an struck a stone, bounced twice, and settled crosswise in the muddy water. His bodyguards looked at one another and slowly laid down their weapons too.

It was Liang Agui who came to escort him downhill. River mud streaked his armor; his left arm was bandaged and an arrow had grazed his cheek. Yao Chang saw him and asked only, “Have they heard the case of your wife’s death?”
“The hearing isn’t finished.”
“Yet you’ve come to arrest me for them?”
“When it is finished, if it is unjust, I’ll still demand an answer.”
“You truly believe they’ll listen?”
Liang Agui held the rope and paused. “First let them hear us once. If we don’t even allow that once, no one will hear anyone ever again.”

Yao Chang watched him, his gaze finally settling on hands smeared with the blood of the wounded. Once, when he commanded troops in Chang’an, he had seen hands like these. He had wanted such men to come to his banner. In the end it was one of them who bound him.

Down in the valley Liang Abao was found among the surrendered wounded. An arrow had entered the side of his abdomen, and he was still bleeding. Liang Agui knelt beside his younger brother and helped the physician press the wound. Feverish and delirious, Abao gripped his brother’s shoulder armor and asked whether they were home yet.
“First we go back to Anding,” Liang Agui said.
“Where’s Sister-in-law?”

His elder brother did not answer. The physician drew out the arrowhead; Liang Abao cried out in pain, calling his brother by the pet name he had used as a child. Those standing around stepped back a few paces without speaking. No order from either army could say the words these two brothers still needed to say.

Three days after the battle, Fu Rong separated and recorded the cases at Anding. Yao’s chiefs, and those who had seized towns or killed officials, were held apart. Civilian laborers driven into the army who had taken no part in killing or pillage were released to their homes. Former Qin deserters were registered under military law, but not condemned wholesale because their surname was Qiang. Du Yan still awaited a military trial. The sentry who killed the two women admitted that the arrows came from his own hands. Fu Rong first allocated support for the two families' children and funeral expenses, so that while the government heard one case the orphans would not have to endure another winter of suffering.

Liang Agui resumed command of his archers. His new service record credited him with stopping cavalry from charging broken Qin units at White Horse Slope and rallying the scattered troops. It also noted that he had left his assigned place in the center without permission, a matter still subject to military review. He could not read it all and asked a clerk to recite it from the beginning. When the clerk reached the field marked “people of origin,” he paused and asked whether it should be filled in. “Write what the old register said,” Liang answered. “Don’t leave it out.” He had never wanted to erase his Qiang identity. He only wanted that, when the drums sounded, no one would draw a sword first because he had seen those two characters.

Yao Chang was escorted east toward Chang’an with no triumphal gate for displaying prisoners. As the guards took him along the Anding road, some people hurled mud at him, while elderly former followers offered the Qiang salute from beyond the crowd. He returned neither greeting nor curse, but looked at each in turn.

Beyond the garrison, Yao Chang saw the names of the battle dead being added to a board on the parade ground. A Di soldier was listed beside a Han, then a Xianbei horseman and a Qiang archer. Nearby people argued about when compensation would be paid, someone demanded an extra day’s battle credit for a comrade, and another was looking for his lost horse. The scene was disorderly. There was nothing solemn or grand about the birth of a new empire.
He watched a long while before asking Fu Rong, “And you call this victory?”
“Enough men died in that valley already,” Fu Rong said.
“What if one day your three seals stop working?”
“Then someone will have to think of another way.”
“Your brother still hasn’t awakened.”
“The court issued grain to the army today.”

Yao Chang asked nothing further. He remembered the banner he had raised at White Grass Valley; at sunset it had once shaded half a hillside. Now the grass had been trampled into mud by the camps. Spring rain would wash it clean, and even the holes where the banner poles had stood might leave no trace.

At Anding’s battlements the watch changed. A junior commandant called the men by name from a register. When he reached a soldier with a Qiang surname, no one looked up. The man answered, “Present,” picked up his bow, and went to his appointed place along the wall. A Han soldier of his company urged him to hurry before their midday meal grew cold.

Beyond the walls, the west wind swept past the furled banners of White Grass Valley and a black Qin flag. The Qin flag carried only a unit number. Each soldier had his own ancestors, his own wounds, names from the past he could not forget. Tonight, at least, they would defend this city together.
